title: Energy-constrained two-way capacities of the pure-loss bosonic channel
abstract: We determine the two-way quantum, entanglement-distribution, private, and secret-key capacities of the pure-loss bosonic channel under an unconditional mean transmitted-photon-number constraint. For transmissivity $η$ and mean photon number $N$, all four capacities coincide and are given by $g(N)-g((1-η)N)$, where $g$ is the entropy of a thermal mode. This resolves the longstanding finite-energy capacity problem by establishing the optimality of the reverse-coherent-information rate introduced in 2009. Our central tool is sector teleportation simulation, which we develop specifically to transfer the input-energy constraint to the shared entanglement resource, thereby preserving the constraint throughout converse arguments for general adaptive protocols. For every $N>0$, we further show that the corresponding strong-converse thresholds coincide with the unconstrained value $-\log_2(1-η)$. For parallel protocols with a hard total-photon-number cutoff, the same finite-energy capacity formula instead satisfies an exponential strong converse. Together, these results establish a unified finite-energy framework for adaptive bosonic communication and reveal how energy constraints fundamentally reshape both attainable rates and converse bounds.
summary: This paper calculates the finite-energy capacity limits for various quantum information tasks (like entanglement distribution and secret key generation) over a pure-loss bosonic channel. By developing a novel 'sector teleportation simulation' technique, the authors prove that these capacities are determined by a simple function of the input energy. This resolves long-standing theoretical questions regarding energy constraints in quantum communication.
main_problem: The paper determines the finite-energy two-way quantum, entanglement-distribution, private, and secret-key capacities of the pure-loss bosonic channel.
main_result: It establishes that all four capacities coincide and are given by a specific function of the input energy $N$ and channel transmissivity $\eta$, resolving the finite-energy capacity problem.
method: The authors use sector teleportation simulation as a central tool to transfer the input-energy constraint to the shared entanglement resource, allowing for rigorous converse arguments for adaptive protocols.
model_or_system: The system analyzed is the pure-loss bosonic channel ($L_\eta$), which models photon loss in optical communication. The analysis is conducted under an unconditional mean transmitted-photon-number constraint.
key_observables: The four capacities ($Q_2, D_2, P_2, K_2$), the regularized relative entropy of entanglement ($E_\infty^R$), and the associated strong-converse thresholds.
important_parameters: Transmissivity $\eta$, mean photon number constraint $N$, and the function $g(x) = (x + 1) \log_2(x + 1) - x \log_2 x$.
main_assumptions: The analysis covers general adaptive protocols with quantum memories, though some results are restricted to parallel inputs with a hard total-photon-number cutoff.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first defining the problem under energy constraints, introducing sector teleportation simulation to maintain the energy budget, deriving the capacity formula $g(N)-g((1-\eta)N)$ for the main results, and then establishing the strong converse bounds.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, unified finite-energy framework for bosonic communication, directly impacting the understanding of achievable rates and fundamental limits in quantum communication channels relevant to quantum optics.

Sector hashing supplies matching achievability, and the operational equivalences Q2 = D2 and P2 = K2 complete the capacity identities. Here cη(N) = g(N) −g((1 −η)N), xi is the unconditional mean input photon number at use i, and ζn is the retained final state after n channel uses.

FIG. 2. Sector teleportation simulation on a fixed total-photon-number subspace. (a) Definition of the independent resource JRBs s,m using an auxiliary optical block A′s and a vacuum environment. The sector pair has m photons on each share; after loss, R still has m photons and Bs has at most m. The environment output is traced out. (b) Alice jointly measures the actual input As and her resource share R, sends the finite outcome a, and Bob corrects Bs. The memories X, Y retain all their correlations. Solid arrows carry quantum systems; the dashed arrow carries the public outcome, also available to Eve. For an input supported on Hs,m, the output is exactly the state in (B1).

FIG. 3. Replica grouping for an adaptive protocol. Each row is an independent copy of the same fixed n-use protocol. The highlighted column groups the ith transmission across r replicas and forms the block of size s = r used in Lemma 6. Gray wires retain the local memories X(j) i , Y (j) i and classical records. The LOCC order and feedback within every row are unchanged. Applying the block inequality column by column and using LOCC monotonicity gives (B55). The limit r →∞ is taken with n and the protocol fixed, before the capacity limit n →∞.
